posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Hello, everyone.
For those who are familiar with both Yahtzee and Poker, I would like your opinion on how to evaluate and compare player rolls against the AI roll when it is head to head and not just trying to complete the Yahtzee type scoring sheet.
So after the player and the AI roll three times, selecting which dice to keep after the first and second rolls, there has to be a comparative “score”.
Combining concepts of both Yahtzee and Poker, here is my initial idea for “scoring” from lowest to highest.
High card
Pair
2 Pair
Small straight (4 sequential numbers out of 5)
3 of a kind
Full house
4 of a kind
Large straight (5 sequential numbers out of 5)
5 of a kind
The only one I am unsure about is where the small straight should fall. Small straights can be fairly common so I don’t want them to be too high in score. So I have moved that around the list and I am still unsure where it fits best.
I appreciate any thoughts you would like to share about how to “score” the results when comparing a player roll against the AI roll.
If you have any questions about the mechanic, I can try to provide more details. But at this time, I am in the exploration and experimenting stage.
Thanks!
EDIT:
I was also wondering if I should include the possibility of both a small straight and a pair at the same time. Since that would technically be possible with 5 dice.
If so, where might that “score” fall?

Yes, Yahtzee uses 5 dice that the player gets to roll up to 3 times. They keep dice they want each time.
1st roll = 5 dice
2nd and 3rd rolls = whatever dice they didn’t decide to keep

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I'm... curious why you aren't just using the Yahtzee scoring rules for all of it?
Yahtzee basically uses the Poker scoring system in its entirety.  So, I'm confused about what you're "taking from poker" and why the scores the actual Yahtzee game don't work for you.
ZombieKidzRule said:
High card
Pair
Click to expand...
These, in Poker, as well as in Yahtzee, are scored based upon "the number".  2 two's is worse than 2 threes.  Yahtzee simply says "count the number of them together and that's the score".
2 two's would just be "four points", while 2 sixes would be "twelve points" in Yahtzee.
3 of a kind and 4 of a kind work on these same rules.
ZombieKidzRule said:
2 Pair
Click to expand...
You could probably score this similarly to the "just count the same number of dice" type rule, or score it slightly under a full house (two pair in Yahtzee is pretty common, after all).
ZombieKidzRule said:
Small straight (4 sequential numbers out of 5)
Click to expand...
Yahtzee scores this as 30 points.
ZombieKidzRule said:
Full house
Click to expand...
25 points.
ZombieKidzRule said:
Large straight (5 sequential numbers out of 5)
Click to expand...
Worth 40 points.
ZombieKidzRule said:
5 of a kind
Click to expand...
You could go either way with this.  50 points as per Yahtzee rules, or you could go with the above rules of "just add up the points" so that 5 sixes is worth more than 5 fours (30 points versus 20).
---
I'm just not sure what it is you're asking for.  The "scoring" rulesets are already very similar or exactly the same between the two games.
If you're using a "random number generator", you'll also have to account for any quirks the program uses for determining "what is random".
As an example:
I designed a "paper" version of Yahtzee for my coworkers (It's about a 10 minute game), where each player is assigned "random dice rolls", and they have to choose where to "spend" those dice.  Each player must contribute 1 dice to each roll, and can't contribute more than 1.  The fifth dice is one I contribute through "random roll" via Excel.
Excel has a high tendency to roll a LOT of 1's and 6's.  2's and 5's are pretty rare.
This usually means I have to "refresh" the Excel document a dozen or more times to get more "reasonable" rolls, rather than getting one member of a team rolling 6 of their 11 dice as 4's, a single 1, two 3's, and 1 five and 1 six.
On a personal note:
I think it's kind of fun that you're trying to turn Board Games into RPG Maker games.
Why?
Because I've been turning Board Games into pen and paper games and TTRPG's (working on a TTRPG of Battleship right now.  Yes, it even has a story, a character generator, and ships that serve as your "class".).

@Tai_MT
Thanks for your response!
My initial post about ordering left out the fact that I was contemplating replacing the numbers on the dice with icons to represent RPG type things like weapons, armor, potions, magic, etc. or to represent actions like attack, block, equip, spell, etc. or to even represent exploration things like dungeon, treasure, event, encounter, town, rest, etc.
That might eliminate the traditional scoring of Yahtzee and focus more on what beats what.
I have been wracking my brain with how to implement such a combo system for RPG combat and maybe exploration. But I keep getting stuck on the why such a convoluted system? And why a challenge between the player and the game?
I could just make a traditional version of either Yahtzee or Poker or still try to combine them with a scoring sheet. But I’m not sure how interesting that would be.
It is something I keep kicking around as an idea that just won’t go away.
So, my initial post was just to work out how that particular list of things would fall in an ordered list as I tried to reason out RPG related possibilities for using the mechanic.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
@ZombieKidzRule
I think if your dice represent "concepts" instead of some value, then the "scoring" system or "rating system" might not make much sense to begin with.  After all, the value of each dice is going to be assigned by the player, rather than the dev.
If I need healing, then rolling 3 potions would be more "valuable" to me than rolling 4 weapons.  Or... however that's meant to work.
If you're looking for "what beats what", then why not either a system of "elements" or a binary system?  I've seen a bunch of dice games use "sword", "shield", and "blank" for its rolls to determine damage and defense in combat.
You might have to nail down what you're hoping to accomplish with the system, first, rather than focusing on what the "rankings" of the symbols on the dice should mean.
I kind of wish I could see what you're envisioning in your head to offer you better advice on getting it off the ground.
I mean, I have "convoluted systems", too, but they're usually in the service of "offering depth" or "offering strategy".
With a dice system where rolls would be random... I'm not sure which part is exciting to you that you would envision some RPG systems playing off of that.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
@Tai_MT
I keep thinking that the reason I can’t come up with anything is because it isn’t a good idea. But yet my mind keeps coming back to it.
It started as an idea of contested rolls. So, only the better roll (player or computer) would get to take action. And you wouldn’t be locked in to only rolling each set on the sheet once. You could choose to roll for whatever set you wanted, but you also had to try to beat the computer’s rolls. And when you finish the sheet, you get something good like gain a level or get a treasure or get to do a special attack or something. So, there would be an incentive to try to finish the sheet.
That was where the what roll set is higher came in.
Then the idea changed to the possibility of the player and computer each getting to do whatever the set they rolled. But the higher set would get a bonus and the lower set would get a penalty or something. You would still have to strategize about trying to get something you want in any given set versus trying to beat the computer versus trying to finish your sheet so you can start another one.
Then I got the idea of the mechanic being a way to randomly determine the game exploration itself. Sort of like if Monopoly had RPG exploration tiles instead of properties. (I’ve put some thought into that idea as well.)
But with each of these ideas, I keep running up against the notion that it is a complex mechanic just to determine what you do in combat.
I think I liked the idea of having to strategize about what set to roll for while still trying to get better than the computer and still trying to get the reward for finishing your sheet.
Kind of like I need to heal or it would be helpful to block or evade the next attack, but I have 3 attack dice showing and that might be my best bet to get a better set than the computer and do more damage.
And I though about there being regular d20 rolls after the set of rolls to make it so whatever you roll isn’t a guaranteed success either.
I thought of several story lines to explain why you might be forced to use such a game play mechanic, but then it still comes down to that question of is it just too complex to be any fun.
And it would be a fair amount of work just to test it out.
And I should mention that I was also toying with the idea of using d8 or d10 instead of d6 so there are more options.
Anyway, that’s sort of the genesis of the original idea and how it morphed. If that makes any sense at all.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Okay, I'm just spitballing here, but let me throw some random ideas that popped into my head at you (even if you don't like them, maybe they can help you refine what you want).
1.  The player selects a "sheet" to complete at the start of each fight (or exploration, or challenge, or whatever).  They get to see what "sheet" the AI has.  The sheet selected might be linked to your equipment, or some defaults, or whatever (however you want to determine access to the sheets up for being chosen".
As an example, the AI has a sheet where they have to roll a 5 of a kind (in anything), but also has to get a Full House of Swords and Shields (either 3 swords and 2 shields, or 3 shields and 2 swords) and a pair of anything.
The player selects a sheet where maybe all they have to complete is a Pair of Shields and a 3 of a kind (anything).
If the player completes their sheet first, they get to deal 1 damage to the AI (or get 1 progress to exploration or a challenge, or whatever) for each challenge on their sheet.
2.  Each challenge on the sheet is an "action" the player can bank.  Lets say at level 1, they can bank 3 actions total.  In the example above, let's say if they get a 3 of a kind in Potions, they banked a Cure, but if they get a 3 in spells, they can bank a Fireball.  The pair of shields means they can bank a "defend 2", which will defend for the round and reduce incoming damage by 2.
Meanwhile, if the AI gets a Full House of 3 swords and 2 shields, it banks an "Attack 3" and a "Defense 2", so that it can do either one.
These are just examples.
3.  The player or the AI could forgo rolling dice on their turn, to spend 1 thing they have banked.  So, if the player banked the Cure, and the AI actually used its turn last round to do 3 damage with "Attack 3", the player could then use their next turn to use the Potion instead of rolling to recover 3 of their missing 5 health.
4.  If a "sheet" is too difficult to finish, there is an option to "reset" the card at the cost of 1 HP and your entire Bank.
---
So, a hypothetical fight might look like this:
Player
Chooses a Sheet that has:
Pair (any)
3 of a Kind (Swords)
Full House (Potions and Spells)
Can bank 3 actions.
AI has a sheet that has:
2 Pair (any)
Small Straight (four different icons)
5 of a Kind (Swords)
Can bank 3 actions.
Player rolls first.
First roll gets them 2 Shields, so they cross of "Pair", and bank a "Defend 2".
Crossing an item off the list, frees up the 2 dice for the remaining 2 rolls.
Second roll gets them 2 Swords, 1 Potion, 1 Spell, and 1 Shield.
Player keeps the Swords.
Third roll gets them the remaining Sword they need.  Cross of "3 of a Kind (Swords)" and bank "Attack 3".
AI rolls next.
First roll nets them Sword, Shield, Spell, Potion, Sword.  Cross of "Small Straight (four different icons)" and bank "Jack of All Trades", which will do 2 damage (1 sword, 1 spell), prevent 1 damage if attacked when it's used, and restore 1 health.
This frees up the 4 dice again for the remaining 2 rolls.
Second roll nets 3 Shields, 1 sword, and 1 spell.
AI keeps 2 Shields.
Third roll nets 1 sword, 1 spell, 1 potion.
Player decides to use their "Attack 3" skill instead of rolling.
3 Damage dealt to AI.  3 of 6 HP remain.
AI rolls again.
First roll nets 2 Potions and 2 spells.  Very lucky!  Crosses off the "2 Pair" and banks a "Cure 2" and a "Fireball 2".
AI is now maxed out.  They could end their turn here so they don't Void out the possible 5 of a kind if they do manage it, or they can attempt to roll for the whole thing.
AI rolls again.
3 Swords!  Very lucky!
Rolls again.
2 more Swords!  EXCEPTIONALLY LUCKY!
AI can't bank the "Attack 5", however, so it's lost to the Void.
AI finished its card, so it deals 3 damage.
Now it can start the card over again.
Player's turn.
Player now has a decision to make.  They could use their Defend 2, and prevent losing their last 2 HP next turn if the AI decides to use one of its banked skills (most likely the banked Jack of All Trades).  Or, they could go for broke and try to finish their card to get the last 3 damage they need to win!
The player likes to live dangerously!
They're a gambler!
Ante up!
Player rolls.  Sword, Sword, Potion, Spell, Shield.
Rotten luck.
Pocket the Potion and Spell.
Roll again.
Shield, Shield, Potion.
Got one thing.  Last roll.  This is gonna be rough.  Either game over or win big!
Last roll.
Potion, Spell.
Player did it!
Card completes, 3 damage dealt to the AI.
AI loses last 3 HP, and goes down.
Player wins!
Gain... however much XP.  Level up!
Does the player want the option for a bigger card to work with?  Maybe new "completion" options to add to their card (oh, you can get access to a "Pair (Treasure)" on this level up!)?  Maybe 2 HP instead?  Whatever you decide is cool for leveling up.
Player is then booted back to the map for more exploring or dungeoneering or maybe a Charisma Challenge.  Whatever.
---
Just spitballin'.  Not sure if that's even in line with what you might have been thinking of.  Hope you get something out of it.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
@Tai_MT
Thanks for those thoughts! Many aspects that you noted have been things I've been contemplating.
I have been thinking that the sheet would always be static for combat, meaning the "set" that is needed to roll to complete a row on the sheet would be the same, but maybe what the "set" represents might change based on the player choice and advancement.
So, picture a traditional Yahtzee sheet and add a few poker combination elements from my original list. To complete a sheet, you have to eventually finish every possible "set" on the sheet, but you can technically repeat "sets" (that just doesn't help you progress in completing the sheet. And because you can always repeat, you can't leave any rows blank like you are forced to do in regular Yahtzee.
And, as I mentioned, the dice being used might be d8 or d10 which expands the sheet possibilities.
I brainstormed lists of combat actions that would be standard for most player classes as well as things they might unlock as they progressed. So, I was thinking of letting the player choose different classes that have different available actions and equipment.
And as the player progressed and unlocked new actions, I was thinking of making some actions a combination where the player gets to choose from more than one.
So, for instance, at the beginning level, the attack (which would have a different icon based on weapon selected) would just be a basic attack. Then, as the player improves, the attack might give the player a choice of a basic attack, a strong attack, or a double attack (each with certain bonuses or penalties to consider).
And I also thought about the banking idea where a defend action might raise armor/defense or have a defense action banked for a future round if you didn't want to take that action in the current round because the computer isn't attacking.
And while I like the concept of the mechanic and the necessity to strategize like your example provides, I always come back to the question is this too complicated and will it remain fun?
I've thought about the "story" premise being that this is a game that is played in a tavern. Or it's a game that is being played by the gods because they're bored. Or it's a game that is being played against the devil for your soul.
All of these might explain why the combat mechanic is so complex instead of just roll d20 to attack and see if you hit.
But then I circle right back to the question of is it going to be fun to actually play?
Since I've already experimented with eventing the initial dice rolling and saving mechanic, I might just have to do a quick mock up on paper with just the computer doing the rolling. (I don't have enough d8 or d10 if I want to use those and I don't feel like going out and buying 4 more sets of dice that I won't use.) Then I can see what it potentially feels like.
A part of me keeps thinking oh, this could be really fun and interesting. But then I start thinking but if you're purposely adding an RPG element to it instead of just completing sheets against the computer, why not just do something simpler?
I mean I could always just make a player versus computer Yahtzee/Poker hybrid with no RPG elements other than changing the dice sides to icons. And just have the sheets show something like the 1's row is potions, the 2's row is swords, the 3's row is shields, etc. And then just have a more traditional scoring system.
Anyway, your thoughts have been very helpful.
I guess I'm just curious if anyone else thinks that this type of concept could actually be fun and worth playing?
And really, I think that is my hang up too. I tend to want to make games that I would want to play and I haven't landed on a solid concept that makes me go OH, YEAH! I would definitely want to play that myself.

kevinkyl said:
This is amazing idea! Wish i can't script, mini game like this seems much more fun to play if able to replace regular combat
Click to expand...
Ha ha, glad you like it.  I'm just piggybacking off of what it sounds like ZombieKidz sort of described with their system.  It would most likely need prototyping and refinement before it'd even be something useful.
@ZombieKidzRule
In my experience, any system could be made "fun".  It's just a matter of testing, refining, and altering.
I would just prototype something and then maybe make some friends play with it.  See where the pain points are.  You could then edit or remove the issues.
I also find that it's less about "how complicated" something might be, and more about "how complicated it feels".
Just as the most recent personal example I have, when I started "changing the rules" for Battleship and having players test it, they were initially very annoyed.  Battleship's rules started changing into like video game format.  What the heck is "Ordinance"?  Why are there "Battlefield Conditions"?  What do you mean the ships can be placed on diagonals this game?  Wait, I get to fire a Nuke for 5 shots (they only got 30 shots to sink all the ships, or as many as possible, in order to keep the game short and under 10 minutes), but it hits a 3x3?
Once the players understood there were two types of "rule changes" (Battlefield Conditions or Available Ordinance), they looked each round to see what the briefing said and decided how to play each round.
I'm also taking it as "good changes of rules" when my players are requesting to change out games they don't like, for Battleship instead.
Testing with players would help you make your systems fun.  You lose nothing by making a mock up and having people play it.  Especially if you get feedback on parts the players are confused by, or note complaints and issues.  You can sometimes even get ideas from the people doing playtesting.
You could always "scale up" the complexity too, like most RPG's do.
Tutorials, ya know
Instead of "information overload", you go "here's a mechanic, play with it a minute, now here's the next".  Iteration!

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
@Tai_MT
Thanks! And I have been intrigued by your messages mentioning your workings on a Battleship type game. I thought that was a pretty cool idea.
Quite a while ago, I started thinking about remaking a very old naval combat game that I played as a child that I think was called Broadside. I remember most of the rules and I recall it being rather fun. I'm still kicking that idea around.
Essentially, it is revolutionary war time period and each ship has a certain number of masts or sails that you put on the plastic hull. The players roll dice to move and turn their ships. And if they are broadside to an enemy, the dice roll can be a canon attack. A hit removes one mast. When all masts are removed, the ship is sunk.
And as I recall, the colonists were protecting merchant ships in the harbor that the British were trying to sink. And there were forts at choke points in the harbor that fired on enemy ships as they passed to get at the anchored merchant ships.
Again, it was pretty fun and seemed like it might be worth converting into some sort of computer board game simulation with some updated rules and concepts.
